At noon the observed latitude was 3° 52' 18" South, and we found a difference of 9' 23" to the north on the reckoning of the distance run by the log, and 34' 23" to the west. The longitude given by the marine watches was, for No. 31, 28° 41' 10", and for No. 38, 28° 39' 18". On board the Naturaliste they signalled us 28° 51', giving a difference of 20' 63" from ours. It is hard enough to account for this difference, the more so as the day before the observations agreed perfectly with one another. In the afternoon it continued to blow a light breeze, but the winds veered towards the east and we had them from east-south-east. I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south-south-east if the winds allowed us to lie that way. By our position at noon we were east and west of the island of Fernando de Noronha at a distance of eighty leagues. Various observations of the variation of the needle gave for mean term, reduced to noon of the day, 8° 36' NW. At sunset the sky turned very hazy, with the look of a good breeze for the night. We also saw some tunny about the ship, but they did not come near enough to give us any hope of taking one. The night of the 25th to the 26th [Frimaire, 16-17 December 1800] was fine but there was little wind. The breeze came to us at times from the east [word struck out, illegible]; it seemed inclined to settle at east-south-east, which allowed us to head south.

1800-12-17.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 26th [Frimaire, 17 December 1800] we had the winds east-south-east and the breeze freshened a little after sunrise. As the weather was fine all day, the decks and between-decks were fumigated with powder and vinegar to drive out the damp and the bad smell the hold water may have brought in. As it had been supposed that the ventilators set up by Citizen Garos by means of his new galley would suffice, no others were shipped to replace them. Obliged to break up those galleys, which could be of no use to us, we had no other resource to make up for what we lacked than the windsails ordinarily used. At noon the observed latitude was 5° 0' 39" South, and we found ourselves five minutes further south than the reckoning gave. The longitude of the marine watches put us at noon in 29° 28' 18" for No. 31, and 29° 18' 31" for No. 38. The reckoned longitude was then 21° 52' 32". In the twenty-four hours there was a difference of 0° 31' 44" to the west. The Naturaliste, being rather too far from us, did not signal these observations. In the evening the weather continued fine but the breeze fell away as the sun went down towards the horizon. From a series of azimuths observed morning and evening with great care, the variation was 7° 21' NW in the evening and 7° 16' in the morning. The night of the 25th to the 26th [17-18 December 1800] was very fine and the sky almost without cloud. We lost sight of the Naturaliste, who answered none of our signals although all night we had our stern light shown from time to time.

1800-12-18.journal_baudin: On the 27th [Frimaire, 18 December 1800] at daybreak we sighted the Naturaliste, who was nearly two [leagues] from us to leeward. As that ship had made us no signal during the night, we had been unable to judge her distance from us. We bore away to close her, and at eight o'clock she was at her usual distance. After sunrise the breeze was rather stronger than it had been during the night, but the winds drew round more to the south-east. In the forenoon the crew were employed serving the cable that had been damaged at the anchorage of Santa Cruz de Tenerife. At noon the observed latitude was 6° 30' 33", and we saw with pleasure that the current might perhaps be beginning to change its set, since for two days we had been finding differences to the south, whereas before they were almost always to the north. That of this day was 17' 33" further south than the reckoning. The longitude given by the watches, reduced to noon, was for No. 31, 29° 46' 3", and for No. 38, 29° 41' 57". The reckoning put us in 21° 55' 2". The Naturaliste signalled us her longitude as usual, but we could never make out her signal; although I let her know it could not be distinguished, she kept it always in the same place. During the evening the sky turned very hazy, and some clouds even gave us a little rain. We were still too far from the coast of America to believe that its nearness caused this change in the atmosphere. At eight in the evening, while we were at the dance, one of those birds the seamen have named the booby came wheeling about the ship and upset the whole order of the dancing. We reckoned it had come to be caught, but after showing itself well it disappeared. The night of the 27th to the 28th [Frimaire, 18-19 December 1800] had nothing remarkable. It blew a light breeze, but the sky was still loaded with cloud and damp.

1800-12-19.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 28th [Frimaire, 19 December 1800], the Naturaliste being about two leagues to leeward of us, we bore away again to close her. It appears that during the night that ship steers freer than we do, and that this is why for two days she has been found so far to leeward every morning. At eight o'clock we had closed her and I made her the signal to steer close-hauled, which she did. In the forenoon the breeze was steady enough, at east-south-east. The sky, which had been much loaded with cloud, became fine, and we found the sea less rough than the day before. At noon the observed latitude was 8° South, whereas our reckoning put us only in 7° 40' 18", so that we no longer had any doubt that the set of the currents had changed, given the large differences to the south we were beginning to find. That of the twenty-four hours was 19' 18", and only 15' 34" to the west. Watch No. 31 gave us for longitude 30° 7' 34", and No. 38, 30° 2' 21". The reckoning by the log was 22° 1' 14". The results of our watches compared with those of the Naturaliste differed by [blank]. In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the breeze fell away as it had been in the habit of doing since we came into the trades. After sunset, however, it freshened a little and was steady enough all through the night, which was very fine and clear. From various azimuths taken morning and evening the mean variation was found to be 6° 38' north-west.

1800-12-20.journal_baudin: On the 29th [20 December 1800] the weather continued fine and the winds were variable from east-south-east towards east, a fresh breeze. We were often obliged to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste, who for two or three days has seemed to sail even worse than usual. In the forenoon we shifted the collar of the stay of our mizzen mast — that is, the stay to the mainmast that holds it — finding it placed far too high. At noon the observed latitude was 9° 36' 2" South, whereas that of the reckoning was only 9° 15' 19", giving a difference of 0° 21'. So there was no longer any doubt that the set of the currents had changed. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 30° 21' 59", and for No. 38, 30° 15' 29", which gave only 19' of westing more than the reckoning, which then put us in 28° 4' 38". The Naturaliste not being within reach to let us know her observations, I made her no signal for them. In the evening the weather continued fine and the sea was rather less hollow than it had been in the morning. From several azimuth observations taken morning and evening, the variation of the magnetic needle was found to be [blank]. After sunset the officer of the watch came to tell me that the jib boom had just carried away. It must have been very rotten indeed, since the wind was very moderate and the breeze light with a smooth sea. It was at once rigged in to be repaired next day. The night of the 29th to the 30th [Frimaire, 20-21 December 1800] had nothing remarkable; the sky was very clear and the winds variable from east to east-south-east. The Naturaliste was kept in sight until midnight, after which she disappeared without making us any signal to show her distance from us. We continued to keep close to the wind under our usual sail. From the 29th to the 30th Frimaire, Year 9, etc. [20-21 December 1800]. On the 30th [Frimaire, 21 December 1800] we had for the greater part of the day the winds east, variable towards east-south-east, a fresh breeze, but the weather was extremely hazy and we got several squalls with rain. In the forenoon, when the crew least expected it, they were all sent aft under the quarterdeck and a general search was then made of the bags and chests in the hope of finding a watch that had been stolen, belonging to Citizen Le Brun. A midshipman was also missing a silver spoon. The search was thorough and even scrupulous; nevertheless nothing was found. These articles being of too small a bulk, whoever took them will have taken care to put them in a safe place. At noon we observed the latitude 11° 11' 10" South, which gave us a difference from the reckoned latitude of 0° 8' 54". The longitude given by watch No. 31 put us in 30° 27' 32", and that of No. 38 in 30° 19' 32". That by the reckoning was 21° 53' 38". In the afternoon the winds stayed east, towards east-south-east, very variable and at times light. The sky turned hazier still than it had been in the morning, and about half past four we had a fairly heavy squall, of rain only. All day the sea had been much agitated with a hollow sea, but towards evening we found it far calmer. During the night of the 30th [Frimaire, 21 December 1800] to the 1st Nivôse [22 December 1800] the sky was now dark and damp and overcast, now very clear. The winds varied as far as east-north-east, but for a short time only. The stern lantern was lit almost all night to show the Naturaliste our position, and I cannot conceive why for three days she has never shown us hers, although she was at a considerable distance.

1800-12-22.journal_baudin: On the 1st Nivôse we had very fine weather all day and the winds held in the quarter variable towards the north. The breeze was even fresh enough, but we found the sea rather rough with a somewhat hollow swell. The Naturaliste being to windward of us, I hauled close to the wind to weather her, but as she did the same we could not get the wind of her until the evening. At noon the observed latitude was 12° 45' South, which gave us a very large difference to the south in the twenty-four hours, since it was 24 minutes. The observed longitude reduced to noon was for No. 31, 30° 14' 9", and for No. 38, 30° 5' 11". The reckoning put us in 21° 50' 38", and we found a difference of 8 minutes to the west. The watches on board the Naturaliste were 3 minutes further east than ours. In the evening we were obliged to change one of our topsail ties, which had already carried away twice. Yet the rope seemed to us sound. From a result of the morning and evening amplitudes compared with the azimuths, the variation of the needle was observed to be 5° 30' NW. During the night of the 1st to the 2nd [Nivôse, 22-23 December 1800] the weather was very fine and the breeze fresh enough, but the Naturaliste's poor sailing prevented us from profiting by it. We often showed our stern lantern to give her our position and learn hers, and as she did not answer us we had to shorten sail to wait until she was in sight.

1800-12-23.journal_baudin: On the 2nd [Nivôse, 23 December 1800] the weather continued fine and the breeze was east, varying to east by north, and rather light. The sea, which the past days had been hollow and rough, became smoother. We held on south-south-east so as to make more way, and to see whether, with the sheets a little eased, the Naturaliste would go better. By the end of the day little difference could be seen. She was, however, less bad than usual and did not fall so far to leeward. In the forenoon we took advantage of the fine weather to set up our fore shrouds, whose deadeyes were nearly together. At noon the observed latitude was 14° 19' 39" South, and we had a difference of 19 minutes 14 seconds to the south. The longitude given by the watches was, by No. 31, 30° 2' 38", and by No. 38, 29° 52' 24". The reckoning put us in 21° 30' 38"; in the twenty-four hours the currents had carried us 13' 29" to the west and 19' 14" to the south. From the mean result of several longitude observations by lunar distances of the sun from the moon, reduced to noon of the 1st Nivôse, we had for west longitude 30° 25' 49", which put us 0° 11' 40" further west than No. 31 gave, which was the one we had been using. In the afternoon, and especially after sunset, the sky turned very hazy and there was even the look of some squalls for the night; the wind, however, did not change, and we did not get the squalls that had made up on the horizon from south-east to north-east.

1800-12-24.journal_baudin: On the 3rd [Nivôse, 24 December 1800] we had the winds east, variable towards the north, and very fine weather all day. In the forenoon we went on setting up the fore shrouds, this work begun the day before not having been finished before the end of the day. In the forenoon a very disagreeable scene occurred on board, which obliged me to send for Citizen Le Brun in my cabin — a man whose sour and unsociable character displeases everyone. After breakfast he had had a quarrel with Citizen Milbert over some pleasantries the latter had made at his expense, at the end of which he threw a glass of water in his face. Citizen Milbert, who was with reason very much offended by so unhandsome a way of answering a joke, would have given him a sound correction had not some of the ship's officers been there to prevent blows. On the report made to me of what had just happened, and having satisfied myself from the depositions of those who had witnessed the affair that Citizen Le Brun was entirely in the wrong, I had him asked to come to my cabin; and as this was not the first complaint laid against him, I told him very seriously that if he went on behaving badly I would put him under arrest in the gunroom and that he would only come out of it to be landed at Mauritius. At noon the observed latitude was 15° 42' South and that of the reckoning 15° 28', so that we again had a difference of 14' to the south. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 29° 44' 45", and for No. 38, 29° 33' 20". By the reckoning it was 21° 8' 38", and by the observation the current had again carried us 10 minutes 48 seconds to the west. On board the Naturaliste the longitude was signalled as 30° 6' 0", which gave a difference, taking a mean of our two watches, of 0° 26' 8". In the evening we took several distances of the sun from the moon, the result of which gave us for mean longitude, over fifteen observations, 30° 6' 15"; so these observations again put us 0° 27' 15" further west than the watches. In the night of the 3rd to the 4th [Nivôse, 24-25 December 1800], the winds having come to us from the north-east, I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south and myself steered that way at eight o'clock.

1800-12-25.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 4th [Nivôse, 25 December 1800] I was informed that during the night the greater part of the men of the port watch had got drunk and that it had not been possible to discover how this debauch had come about; but that among them some were so drunk that two came onto the quarterdeck, where, in the presence of the officer of the watch and all the quartermasters' mates, they set about breaking open the midshipmen's daily provision chest. When Citizen Le Bas was up I had a general search made, and after much looking it was found that they had drunk part of a small cask of Tenerife wine belonging to Citizen Le Brun, which they had discovered in the between-decks although it was well stowed among other goods. When I was satisfied that this was how they had got drunk, the whole watch was condemned to drink water until the cask was full again, and then to eight days on water for having been drunk. This last penalty applied only to the men who were drunk. In the forenoon we had very fine weather and the winds east-north-east, variable to north-east, which allowed us to steer full and by to the south-east. At noon the observed latitude was 17° 26' 54", which gave us a difference of 29' to the south beyond the reckoning. The longitude given by the marine watches was, for No. 31, 28° 47' 25", and for No. 38, 28° 34' 46". The reckoned longitude put us in 20° 14' 38", and there had been in the twenty-four hours a difference of 12' 34" to the west. In the evening the weather continued fine and it blew a fresh breeze. At sunset the sky turned extremely hazy, and although the night was clear enough we got about midnight a heavy shower of rain without any increase of wind, which lasted more than half an hour, after which the sky became fine again.

1800-12-26.journal_baudin: On the 5th [Nivôse, 26 December 1800] we had the winds north-east and north-east by east, a fresh breeze. The sky was somewhat hazy and we had now and then a few small showers of rain, but of little consequence. In the forenoon part of the after hold was broken out to get at some casks of vegetables stowed there which we needed. During this work the ship lost much of her way and the Naturaliste, for the first time since the beginning of the voyage, gained on us, although we made more sail as she came up. The officer of the watch, Citizen Baudin, whose carelessness of his duties as a seaman is beyond anything one can imagine, put me so much out of humour that I was obliged to take part of his watch. I had already warned this officer that it was my intention that those on watch should, during that time, keep the conduct and bearing proper to such a duty. This one, however, almost always taken up while he is on deck with idle or at best useless things, and having no longer the means of amusing himself with the midshipmen of his watch, with whom he kept up a conversation always harmful to the good of the service, was this time busy drawing, leaning carelessly on the capstan. I found him so on coming out of my cabin, having watched him for some minutes. When he caught sight of me he put away his work and I went back in. Half an hour later I came out again and found him still busy with his drawing. Then, without saying anything to him, I took the watch and had the sails trimmed to the wind, which he ought to have done two hours before. I reserve for my arrival at Mauritius to let this officer know how dissatisfied I am with his conduct on watch. Although he knows where he stands on that head from all I have already said to him, there is every reason to believe we shall be obliged to part company if he does not change over the passage that remains to us. At noon the observed latitude was 18° 59' 9" South, which gave us 12' 15" of difference to the south. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, [blank], and for No. 38, 27° 0' 9". That of the reckoning put us in 18° 59' 9". The currents [blank]. In the afternoon the after part of the ship was restowed where it had been disturbed in the morning, and at once the Naturaliste returned to her station, that is, astern and to leeward. At sunset we had a slight shower of rain and some mist with a little wind, but both were of short duration and the sky became clear. The night of the 5th to the 6th [Nivôse, 26-27 December 1800] was fine enough despite a very hazy sky and clouds that did not look well. There was little wind.

1800-12-27.journal_baudin: On the 6th [Nivôse, 27 December 1800] the winds were east-north-east in puffs, the sky much overcast and at times rainy, or rather misty. In the forenoon the ship was cleaned and fumigated from forward aft, and water was let into the hold to renew what was there, as it was beginning to smell bad. At noon the observed latitude was 20° 7' 33" South and this time we found no difference at all from the reckoning. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 26° 24' 21", and for No. 38, 26° 8' 53". The reckoning put us in 17° 49' 38", and, as with the latitude, we found no difference. Our position at noon laid down on the chart put us within sight of the Martin Vaz islets, and we should surely have sighted them had the longitude assigned to them been right. But we were the less surprised not to meet with them since, by Lapérouse's observations, they lie in 20° 30' 35" of latitude and 30° 30' of longitude, which put them about sixty leagues from us to the west by south-west. In the afternoon the breeze was very light and the wind unsteady. The sky, though fine, turned very hazy, and we had at times some misty clouds that gave us a little rain. The result of two amplitudes, morning and evening, gave for the mean variation of the two observations 5° 34' 12" NW. After sunset we had a few small squalls with rain and wind, which were of short duration. During the night of the 6th to the 7th [Nivôse, 27-28 December 1800] the wind was very uneven and often attended by misty clouds that brought some fairly strong gusts, but which were followed by a calm as soon as they had passed us. We carried very little sail all night to wait for the Naturaliste, who was at a considerable distance, though we had her in sight by the moonlight when the sky was clear.

1800-12-28.journal_baudin: On the 7th [Nivôse, 28 December 1800], as soon as it was light we sighted a large ship to leeward of us, about two leagues off. The Naturaliste, who was far to leeward, seeing that we made her no signal about it, reported her to us, no doubt believing we had not seen her. As that ship appeared to be running north-north-west, we judged she might be an American bound for the continent. In the forenoon the winds were north-east but very unsteady. We were now becalmed, now making five and six miles under squalls that did no more than pass over and followed one another quickly. The sky would then be darkened by a kind of very damp mist, and a quarter of an hour later it could not be finer. At noon, as we were taking the altitude, one such cloud took the sun's light from us and we could get no observation of latitude. In the evening the same squalls came on again, but they were less frequent. At sunset we closed the Naturaliste, who was far to leeward. It seemed to me that although the winds allowed us to lie full and by to the south-east, that ship was steering some other course. The night of the 7th to the 8th [Nivôse, 28-29 December 1800] had nothing remarkable. The winds were light and very unsteady. At times we had a fine sky, but more often it was covered with misty clouds that gave us a soft, light rain which did our plants a great deal of good.

1800-12-29.journal_baudin: On the 8th [Nivôse, 29 December 1800] the greater part of the day passed in calm, or at least with so little wind that we made very little way. What breeze there was proved extremely variable from east to south-east and even to south-south-east, which made the Naturaliste fall much further to leeward than usual. All through the forenoon the sky was very fine, though hazy, but about eleven o'clock a cloud came up which, obscuring the sun for more than three quarters of an hour, prevented us from observing its altitude, while the whole horizon all round was of a remarkable beauty. In the evening we met with a heavy swell from the south, which made us fear we should have the winds from that quarter. At sunset the sky turned very hazy and we were almost becalmed. During the night of the 8th to the 9th [28-29 December 1800] the breeze was rather steadier and the winds held in the quarter from east-north-east to east, a light breeze. We had at times some small misty clouds, but they soon cleared away and gave little wind. We were often obliged to make various changes in our sails to wait for the Naturaliste, who was rather too far astern. The southerly swell that had begun to be felt in the evening grew heavier, and everything led us to believe we should have the winds from that quarter next day.

1800-12-30.journal_baudin: On the 9th [Nivôse, 30 December 1800] the breeze was very light and the winds extremely variable from east towards north and from east towards south. The sea, though smooth, was disturbed by a fairly heavy swell from the south which foretold winds from that quarter, or showed that they must have been blowing pretty hard there. About nine o'clock the Naturaliste signalled us several splits in her sails which she was going to repair at once, and as soon as we had answered her she took in her topgallant sails and main topsail, which obliged us in turn to shorten sail. At two in the afternoon she was in a state to go on under all plain sail, and we did the same. At noon the observed latitude was 23° 13' 42", so that we had the sun almost in the zenith. A singular enough remark is that since crossing the Line we had not had a single hot day, even at the times when there was least wind. The hygrometer, which had always stood above 90°, showed clearly that there was a great deal of moisture in the air, but we should never have imagined the quantity could be large enough to absorb so great a part of the sun's rays, towards which we were advancing each day; and yet when we were nearest to it the thermometer stood steadily at 17 and 18°. For two days we had been unable to observe the sun's meridian altitude, which, although the horizon was fine, was wrapped in cloud at that hour. That of this day was 23° 13' 42", which gave us in 72 hours a difference of 10 minutes 15 seconds to the south. The observed longitude was for No. 31, 26° 15' 42", and for No. 38, 25° 56' 17". The difference which the longitude of the watches gave us over these three days against the reckoning was far more considerable than the one we had to the south, since it was found to be 1° 0' 45" to the west — proof that the currents had not yet left us, as we had hoped from the small difference given by the last two observations. In the evening as in the night there was little wind, and the sea continued swelly from the south. The sky was fairly hazy and the very variable winds came at times as far round as south-south-east, almost calm.

1800-12-31.journal_baudin: On the 10th [Nivôse, 31 December 1800] the winds continued extremely variable and we had a very light breeze. In the morning we found that the southerly swell had increased considerably during the night, and all day we had a heavy sea, long and hollow, which did not promise fine weather and which would have tried the ship greatly had it blown a strong breeze. But as we were making little way we were not incommoded by it. About nine o'clock we had a light rain that lasted more than an hour and which, without being very heavy, still wetted through all the men of the watch. There was very little wind while it lasted, and less still when it had passed. At noon the observed latitude was 24° 2' 12" South, and we found no difference at all to the south from the reckoned latitude. The difference to the west by the result of the watches was almost as nil, for it was only 29 seconds. The longitude given by No. 31 was 26° 5' 29", and by No. 38, 25° 41' 41". That of the reckoning was then [blank]. At two in the afternoon we had a second squall which gave us more rain than the first and lasted longer too, without wind. For the rest of the day the weather was very unsettled and the winds extremely variable. We observed that since we had passed the sun the squalls always brought us calm, whereas those we had before reaching it gave us puffs that made us go a little way. In the night of the 10th to the 11th [Nivôse, 31 December 1800 - 1 January 1801] the sky became very fine and clear after moonrise, but what little breeze there was meant we made little southing. The heavy sea we had found that morning had become much less long and hollow, and the sea became smooth.

1801-01-01.journal_baudin: On the 11th [Nivôse, 1 January 1801], from the morning the little wind we had from the eastward fell away as the sun rose above the horizon, and everything foretold that the greater part of the day would pass in calm, as indeed it did, for at noon the ship would hardly steer, and after noon we were in a flat calm, obliged to clew up our courses. In the forenoon we took advantage of the fine weather to have the crew's clothes and hammocks put out to air, for they had taken the damp the day before, and I was obliged, with the officers, to see it done; for the surgeon-major whom we have in charge on board occupies himself with anything but his trade. As he is a maker of phrases and pamphlets, he is no doubt preparing some new production which he will not fail to send to the press by the first opportunity. I had put off until this day entering his daily conduct in my journal, being persuaded that the various warnings I have given him would bring about some change; but as he goes on as he began, and as his self-esteem suffers at being shipped as a surgeon, regarding that station as beneath him, I shall have patience until Mauritius, where I shall explain to him so plainly the conduct he is to keep on board that, if it does not suit him to conform to my intentions as to his duties, he shall be free to land — or, to put it better, I shall land him, even against his will. At noon the observed latitude was 24° 54' 18", which gave us a difference of 8 minutes to the south from the reckoning. The longitude by watch No. 31 was [blank], and by No. 38, 25° 31' 53". The reckoned longitude was then 16° 43'. The whole afternoon passed in calm, as did the greater part of the night, during which the sky was very fine.

1801-01-02.journal_baudin: On the 12th [Nivôse, 2 January 1801] we were no better off for wind than the day before, and it continued calm or nearly so until sunset. We employed our time on various jobs, and above all in cleaning the ship's outside, which already had much weed and barnacles fast to her wales. The small boat was put in the water for this. If the day was a blank for our progress, it was not so for natural history, for we took several very curious objects — among others a small marine animal in the shape of a lizard which seemed to us quite new, but which to our great regret we found described by M. de la Martinière in Lapérouse's voyage. As the description that naturalist gave of it is very exact, we could not be mistaken; but it is not the same with the engraving, which departs from it greatly. The drawing I give of it is much more exact, and it would be a pity that so pretty an animal should be known only by its description. Among the most curious objects we took, after the little animal I have just spoken of, is the Nautilus spirula, of which Linnaeus's description gives an idea, but which, though agreeing in several characters, differs in many others. I shall make particular mention of it in the journal of the voyage. We also took various species of Physsophora hydrostatica, which have been drawn in their natural colours and as true to life as it was possible to make them; for it is no easy thing to paint marine animals with all their detail and their brilliance. At noon the observed latitude was 24° 55' 35" South. The longitude given by No. 31 was at that noon 25° 31' 15", and that of No. 38, 25° 7' 45". The reckoning put us in 16° 22' 30" at the same hour. Neither the observation nor the watches gave any difference from the reckoning, so the current we had met with so constantly appeared to have ceased. In the evening the calm continued until sunset, when a light air came to us from south to south-south-east. During the night the weather was very fine, and the winds having drawn round to the south-east we went onto the port tack, signalling the Naturaliste to do the same; she was then half a league from us to leeward.

1801-01-03.journal_baudin: On the 13th [Nivôse, 3 January 1801] the winds were nearly as calm as the day before and we made little way. This day, on which we had founded great hopes for natural history, was not a fortunate one, for everything we took in molluscs or other objects was like what we had already gathered. We met with no more of those little lizard-like creatures that were so pretty and singular, as may be seen from the very exact drawings I have given of them in the abridged journal. All we met with that was new was a kind of jellyfish, extremely pretty but which it is not possible to draw from what remains of it. At noon the observed latitude was 25° 22' South, and the longitude by the watches put us, for No. 31, in 25° 17' 15", and for No. 38, in 24° 52' 9". That of the reckoning gave 16° 30'. The small difference we had from the reckoning confirmed that the strength of the current was much diminished, or rather nil. The Naturaliste being rather too far off, we could not compare the results of our timekeepers. About eight in the morning the winds had drawn round to east-south-east, variable to east, and the breeze had freshened a little; but in the afternoon it fell calm again and we made very little way. Some moments after sunset the Naturaliste, for whom we were waiting and who had closed us considerably, put a boat in the water; and as it drew well away from the ship we thought it was coming aboard, which made me heave to. But seeing it turn back after going a good quarter of a league from its ship, it appears something had been seen on the water and they had gone to find out what it might be. As that ship made us no signal, it can have been nothing much. The night of the 13th to the 14th [Nivôse, 3-4 January 1801] was fine and the wind still calm, or at least so light that it came to much the same thing. The sky was often hazy and seemed to promise wind, but it all cleared away without giving any.

1801-01-04.journal_baudin: On the 14th [Nivôse, 4 January 1801] the breeze was still very light and we made little way. The winds varied from east to north-east in the forenoon, and in the evening they came round as far as north-north-east; but they had no strength in them and we went very little ahead. We flattered ourselves, however, that we had reached the region of the variable winds, in which we hope to find winds that will make up for the little we have met with until now. All day the sky was very fine. For all our watchfulness to see whether some mollusc of a new species might pass along the ship, we saw none that could hold our attention, and even the species we had met with on the preceding days had disappeared. At noon the observed longitude was [blank] for watch No. 31 and 24° 12' 48" for No. 38. The observed latitude had been found at noon to be 26° 5', which gave us a difference of one minute from the reckoning, so that the current we reckoned ourselves rid of still existed, only with less force. In the afternoon we made various shiftings in the hold to get at several articles of consumption we needed. They told considerably on the ship's sailing, since, under almost equal canvas, the Naturaliste passed ahead of us. It was, I think, the second time that had happened to her since our departure from France, and it will perhaps be the last once we have restowed what we have broken out. During the night of the 14th to the 15th [Nivôse, 4-5 January 1801] there was little wind. The sky was very hazy and nevertheless fine. The winds went round to the south-west, which persuaded us that we had the general winds from south-east and east behind us.

1801-01-05.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 15th [Nivôse, 5 January 1801] the Naturaliste was more than two leagues ahead of us and to windward. I do not know why, during a night that was often fine despite various squalls that made up on the horizon, she was allowed to draw so far off. Be that as it may, after sunrise she clewed up her courses to wait for us, which she might well have spared herself, for we should not have been long in joining her. At nine o'clock she made us a signal which, for all our attention, could not be made out, and which she hauled down half an hour later. At eleven o'clock, the wind having freshened a little, we had soon weathered her, and she had no other advantage left than being about a league to windward. In the forenoon several squalls made up on the horizon, which did not last long. We got some of them, which gave a little rain without much wind. At noon the observed latitude was 26° 33' 9". The longitude by watch No. 31 was 24° 23' 42", and by No. 38, 25° 56' 22". The reckoning put us in 14° 47' 30". On board the Naturaliste they signalled us 24° 31'. In the afternoon I signalled the Naturaliste that I had been unable to make out the signal she had made me in the morning; and as she mistook my question, or made out the flag wrongly, she took it for an order to close, so that she very quickly lost the small advantage she had gained in passing ahead of us. As the sky did not look well and there was the appearance of squalls and wind for the night, we furled the topgallant sails and took a reef in each topsail. I let the Naturaliste know before sunset that the course would be south-east if the winds, then south with a good breeze, drew aft during the night. As that ship did not hold her wind, we were obliged to bear away two points and a half to close her. In the night of the 15th to the 16th [Nivôse, 5-6 January 1801] it blew a fresh breeze from south to south-east and we went on running east, keeping close to the wind. There were now and then a few small squalls, but of little consequence. By the result of the watches reduced to noon, we found the currents had carried us 14 minutes to the west.

1801-01-06.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 16th [Nivôse, 6 January 1801] the breeze was rather stronger and the sea somewhat rough, with a disposition to get up. After sunrise, the Naturaliste being far to leeward, we bore down on her to close her. In the forenoon the breeze increased, but it began to fall away as soon as the sun had passed the meridian. At noon the observed latitude was 26° 6' 5". The longitude given by No. 31 was 22° 48' 4", and by No. 38, 22° 19' 18". That of the reckoning put us in 12° 44' 0". From a series of twelve observations by lunar distances of the sun from the moon, the mean longitude was found to be 28° 38' 55" reduced to noon, which gave a difference from No. 31, the one we ordinarily used, of only 9' 9" further east than that watch. In the evening the winds were east-south-east, not strong, though the sky was loaded with cloud and there were several squalls on the horizon. We went on lying close-hauled on the east tack to reduce our longitude a little. At sunset we took a reef in each topsail and in the mizzen topsail, and closed the Naturaliste again, who was carrying much freer than we were. In the night of the 16th to the 17th [Nivôse, 6-7 January 1801] a few squalls passed over which brought a great deal of damp that made the air cold, but there was little wind. The sea was nevertheless beginning to get up, and there was no appearance of fine weather for the morrow.

1801-01-07.journal_baudin: On the 17th [Nivôse, 7 January 1801], at six in the morning, the winds seeming settled in the south-east, I signalled the Naturaliste to alter course and lie close-hauled on the port tack. I did the same myself and we both wore ship. In the forenoon the weather turned very bad and squally. As the sea, which we took head on, came very high, I had a second reef taken in the mizzen topsail and the topgallant masts struck. In the course of the forenoon, however, the sky became fine, but it blew hard until noon. The winds had drawn round to east-south-east. The observed latitude at noon was 25° 46' 2". Preparations had been made to take several lunar distances of the sun from the moon, which we could not observe, any more than an hour angle to learn the way we had made in longitude. The difference in the twenty-four hours was, by the log, [blank]. In the afternoon the sky was very fine and the breeze fell away a great deal. The sea too became smoother, and the look of bad weather we had had in the morning disappeared entirely. At sunset the variation of the needle was observed to be [blank] by an amplitude at setting. At seven o'clock we bore down on the Naturaliste, who was far to leeward, to close her and keep her in sight during the night. That ship, to make more way, always carried a point or two freer than we did. In the night of the 17th to the 18th [Nivôse, 7-8 January 1801] the winds varied from east-south-east to east and the breeze was steady enough. The sky cleared quite fine and the sea was smooth enough.

1801-01-08.journal_baudin: On the 18th [Nivôse, 8 January 1801] we had a very fine breeze from the east and a clear sky all day, which gave us the opportunity of checking our longitude observations by taking fresh distances, which, reduced to noon of the day, gave 21° 35' 45". The longitude of No. 31 reduced to the same moment was 22° 4' 37", and that of No. 38, 21° 33' 27". The observed latitude was 26° 58' 26", which gave us little or no difference from that of the reckoning; but by the result of No. 31 we found the currents had carried us 31' 3" to the west in forty-eight hours, having had no observation of latitude the day before. In the forenoon decks were cleared generally and the ship was fumigated throughout. All the hammocks were also washed and spare ones issued until those just washed were dry. In the course of the evening the weather was fine, the winds east with a light breeze and a smooth sea. In the night of the 18th to the 19th [Nivôse, 8-9 January 1801] the sky for some hours did not look well, but after moonrise it all cleared away and turned fine again. The Naturaliste being rather far off, a light was shown for her to which she did not answer. At midnight, however, that ship was seen a little ahead of us. We then went on watching her and saw that she was keeping much too close to the wind, and that this was the chief reason why she made so little way and made us lose still more.

1801-01-09.journal_baudin: On the 19th [Nivôse, 9 January 1801] the weather continued fine and the winds in the course of the day drew a little from east towards north. We should have made a fair run in these twenty-four hours had they steered on board the Naturaliste on the course indicated, and had that ship, instead of keeping her sails always shaking in order to work to windward, borne away a point to go faster. In order to show Captain Hamelin the bad seamanship practised on board his ship, especially at night, I had every sail set, which obliged him to bear away and consequently to make some way. In the forenoon we took fresh distances, the result of which will be found on the log table when they have been worked out. At noon the observed latitude was 28° 30' 27", which gave little difference from the reckoning. By the result of watch No. 31 we were at noon in 21° 30' 23", and by No. 38 in 20° 57' 44". The longitude by the observation of the sun's distance from the moon was 21° 16' 15", which gave 0° 14' 8" of difference to the east from No. 31. That of the reckoning was 11° 5', and we no longer had any hope that a current contrary to the one we had experienced would win back for us the way it had made us lose. In the afternoon we went on crowding sail to force the Naturaliste to keep her sails full and not amuse herself hugging the wind. The weather was very fine and the sea foretold calm. The breeze was even beginning to fall away. During the night we had to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste. The weather stayed fine but there was little wind.

1801-01-10.journal_baudin: On the 20th [Nivôse, 10 January 1801], during the day the winds varied from east to north-east and the breeze was fine. Had the Naturaliste been able to keep up with us we should have made a good run in these twenty-four hours; but though she was covered with sail and we had only the foresail and topsails, how could she follow us? In the forenoon all the crew's spare clothing was put out to air, so that the ship looked like a clothing manufactory in which one might have found every shape and every colour. At noon the observed latitude was 29° 43' 9". The longitude by watch No. 31 was 20° 55' 36", and by No. 38, 20° 1' 24". Citizen Bissy, our astronomer, gave me for the first time since our departure the result of a longitude observation by a lunar distance of the moon from the sun, which, reduced to noon of this day, gave 19° 48' 0"; referred to the rate of No. 38, which he ordinarily uses, it differed by 0° 13' 24" to the east. In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the winds drew round to the north-east. From various azimuths taken morning and evening, the variation of the needle was found to be 8° 50' NW. The night of the 20th to the 21st [10-11 January 1801] had nothing remarkable. The winds drew round to the north, very light, and we went on steering south-east, keeping in sight of the Naturaliste, who was a little astern.

1801-01-11.journal_baudin: On the 21st [Nivôse, 11 January 1801], at daylight the Naturaliste was very far astern of us, although we had carried no sail during the night. As that ship was well to windward, it seemed to us she had not steered south-east. It had been noticed that for two days that ship did not follow the course indicated during the night. This was losing ground to no purpose, especially when the wind was not free. I do not know whether it is for the small pleasure of being to windward of us in the morning that such a manoeuvre is made. In the forenoon it blew a fresh breeze, and as usual we could not profit by it, having to wait for the Naturaliste. At noon the observed latitude was 31° 3' 0" South and the longitude of the watches reduced to noon was, for No. 31, 19° 10' 45", and for No. 38, 18° 35' 53". By the reckoning we ought to have been in 8° 32'. The difference given by the observation was 9' to the south and 0° 4' 21" to the west. After the sun's observation at noon I steered SE by E and made the signal to the Naturaliste, who probably will not have seen it given the distance she was at; but as she fell into our wake she must have seen that we had changed course from south-east to south-east by east. In the evening the breeze fell away a great deal and the stillness of the sea made us fear a calm. The course of the day was a fortunate one for natural history. We took several species of mollusc, one among others bearing a great resemblance to a set of organ pipes, and we gave it that name. We have found it described in Linnaeus under the name Salpa maxima. The fish were of the kind called Diodon holocanthus. But the most interesting thing we took was the Nautilus spirula wrapped in the mollusc in which it is found, and which I have had drawn from life. In the night of the 21st to the 22nd [Nivôse, 11-12 January 1801] the winds were the same and the breeze light. We held on south-east by east under little sail to give the Naturaliste time to join us.

1801-01-12.journal_baudin: On the 22nd [Nivôse, 12 January 1801] the winds varied from north by east to north-east by north and the breeze was very light all the forenoon. At daylight the Naturaliste was far to leeward of us, which led us to suppose she had not seen the signal announcing the course south-east by east, which is very likely. But as she had come into our wake the day before and had steered the same course as ourselves, I did not think she could have imagined we should steer south-east during the night. In the forenoon we took a dozen fish of the kind we had chased the day before, and almost all proved to be of the same size. Although the drawing I give of them is in their natural colours and perfectly well executed, several were stuffed and others put into spirits. At noon the observed latitude was 31° 45' 20" South and the reckoned longitude 7° 8' 9". That of No. 31 was 17° 48' 25", and No. 38 gave 17° 11' 22". During the evening the breeze was a little fresher than in the morning, but it fell away as the sun went down towards the horizon. The mean of two amplitudes and two azimuths gave for the variation of the magnetic needle 8° 24' north-west. The night of the 22nd to the 23rd [Nivôse, 12-13 January 1801] had nothing remarkable. There was little wind, and the Naturaliste having closed us within sight, we held the same course. In the middle of the night a very heavy swell from south to south-south-east began to be felt; and as this sea took us abeam, both the ship and ourselves were somewhat incommoded by it.

1801-01-13.journal_baudin: On the 23rd [Nivôse, 13 January 1801] the winds were the same as the day before and the breeze fresh enough. After sunrise we sighted a sail to windward of us, bearing north-east. The distance we were at did not allow us to make out what ship she might be nor what course she was steering. In the forenoon I was informed by the chief medical officer on board that Citizen Millebert had passed an extremely troubled night, and that several times it had been necessary to wake him to calm the agitation caused him by his regret at being parted from his wife, his children and indeed all his family. For a long time it had been noticed that he had grown extremely melancholy, and the doctor, fearing this might tell on his health, begged me to speak to him in a way that would set his mind at rest. It is no doubt hard at sea to make cheerful a man who takes pleasure in being melancholy, and often all one can say to him only makes him feel more keenly the privations he is forced to bear. Nevertheless I asked Citizen Milbert to come to my cabin, and I used every means to let him know how sorry I was to see him in a state that could not but become fatal to him. After we had parted, I was told of one of the causes contributing to increase his anxieties. Someone — who no doubt had reproaches to make himself over his own conduct — had put it into his head that at the time of our departure from Tenerife I had written to the Minister of Marine about him in unflattering terms. I was at first astonished that he could have believed it, and I reproached him in a friendly way for not having told me of it sooner. It seemed to me the most straightforward course was to show him my letter, and I read it to him in full. I hope this condescension on my part will restore his cheerfulness, and I shall count myself very fortunate if it helps to do so. About eleven o'clock we saw an albatross, or more commonly a Cape sheep. This meeting was a subject of amusement, but it lasted little, for the bird, after going once or twice round the ship, disappeared. At noon the observed latitude was 32° 26' South and the reckoned longitude 6° 50' west. That given by watch No. 31 was 16° 9' 55", and that of No. 38, 15° 32' 47". During the evening there was little wind, and the swell we had met with in the night had increased greatly and caused us considerable rolling, as it took us abeam. At four in the afternoon I signalled the Naturaliste to steer east-south-east and headed that way myself. During the night the weather was fine and the breeze rather light. The heavy swell we had had for twenty-four hours began to go down.

1801-01-14.journal_baudin: On the 24th [Nivôse, 14 January 1801] we had a fine breeze from north-north-east to north-north-west and fine weather. Alone we should have made a great deal of way, but as we had to wait for the Naturaliste the run of the twenty-four hours was small for the wind there was. In the forenoon an albatross that was sitting on the water passed near the ship and was fired at from on board. I sent the boat for it, and it was handed to Citizen Maugé to skin. Its flesh, which I had dressed as a salmi, was generally found good, and although the table was well served nothing was left of the dish. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 1' South and the reckoned longitude 5° west. The longitude given by No. 31 was [blank] and that of No. 38, 13° 32' 52". In the afternoon the winds drew round to north-north-west and the breeze freshened a little until sunset. The sea was driven by a heavy swell from west-north-west which led us to judge that it had blown hard from that quarter in these parts. The variation of the needle, from the result of an amplitude at sunset and an azimuth after sunrise, gave 9° 6' north-west. During the night of the 24th to the 25th [Nivôse, 14-15 January 1801] the weather was very hazy with much damp in the air; nevertheless it was fine, and the Naturaliste, who was near enough to us, could carry all sail.

1801-01-15.journal_baudin: On the 25th [Nivôse, 15 January 1801] the weather continued fine and the breeze, which was north-north-west and fresh enough, carried us a little to the east. In the forenoon the ship was cleaned and fumigated throughout, and a general inspection was made of the state of the crew's clothing. That of several needing repair was handed to the tailor with pieces of cloth to put it in a serviceable state. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 5' South and the reckoned longitude 2° 25' west. That of watch No. 31 put us in 11° 31' 55", and No. 38 in 10° 52' 37". As the observations of the 24th were doubtful, having been set about too late to be had with accuracy, we found that in the forty-eight hours the currents had carried us 0° 5' 51" to the south and 6° 15' 42" to the east. In the afternoon it continued to blow a fresh breeze, but the sky turned hazy and extremely charged with vapour. The horizon in various quarters was ringed with great dark black clouds that did not look well. The night, however, was fine, and the Naturaliste, so as not to lose ground, furled only her royals. By an amplitude at sunset the variation of the needle was found to be 9° 53' north-west. This observation does not deserve much confidence. The heavy swell from west-north-west that we had had for two days began to go down and the sea gave no sign of bad weather. During the day we saw several albatrosses and two or three storm petrels.

1801-01-16.journal_baudin: On the 26th [Nivôse, 16 January 1801] the weather was bad all day, although the wind stayed south-south-west and moderate. At sunrise the whole horizon was extremely dark and loaded with great black clouds, so that we hardly knew from where the wind would come. The barometer, which had fallen three lines, gave us clear enough warning of the change that was preparing, and we were in a state to bear it should it turn bad in the course of the day. At seven o'clock, as the worst appearance was in the south, I had a reef taken in the mizzen topsail and the mizzen topgallant mast struck, being useless to us. The halliards of the lower yards were also rove. Shortly afterwards it came on to rain. The winds during the squall came to west and south-west, where they stayed for the rest of the day. Although we often had light puffs with mist, the Naturaliste, in order to close us, took in none of her sails. At noon there was a clear interval that allowed us to observe the latitude. It was found to be 32° 59' South. The reckoned longitude at noon was [blank]. As there was no hour angle this day, we could not learn by our timekeepers how far we had advanced to the east. After the sun's observation I signalled the Naturaliste the course east-south-east and steered that way myself. During the evening the weather was no finer than in the morning. We had alternately a misty rain and fine weather. The slight motion of the sea, however, did not positively foretell bad weather, and the clouds, though fairly low, did not drive with any great speed, from which we concluded that the middle region of the atmosphere was calm enough. Before sunset, our horizon being far from fine, I had a reef taken in each topsail, and everything was made ready so as not to be embarrassed in the night should it turn bad. In the night of the 26th to the 27th [Nivôse, 16-17 January 1801] the weather was better than the look of it promised. It blew a fresh breeze from south-south-west, and alone we should have made a great deal of way.

1801-01-17.journal_baudin: On the 27th [Nivôse, 17 January 1801] the winds were south-south-west with a fresh breeze, but the sky was not fine and the barometer promised no fine weather. In the forenoon I had our lower-mast preventer backstays got up and fitted, so as to have only to put them in place should circumstances require it. The sea, which had smoothed in the night of the 25th to the 26th [Nivôse, 15-16 January 1801], became swelly again and the ship was tried by a heavy sea which we judged must give us a fairly large difference to the north, and perhaps to the east as well. Our conjectures were true up to a point, for at noon the observed latitude was 32° 55' 56" South, whereas by the course we had run it should have been much greater; so we found a difference to the north of 0° 16' 0". The longitude given by watch No. 31 was 6° 6' 4", and that of No. 38, 5° 25' 23". By the reckoning we were 2° 49' 24" east of the meridian of Paris. During the day we saw neither albatrosses nor petrels such as we had met with on the preceding days. But several people were positive they had seen two or three different species of fucus pass along the ship. As I did not see them, I do not know what species they may be, supposing there was no mistake; for from the way they have been described, I know of no species of fucus to which they can be referred. In the evening it continued to blow a fresh breeze from south-south-west. In a squall that did not last long the winds drew round to the east, but they came back at once to south-west by south. I signalled the Naturaliste the course south-east by east and headed that way myself. After sunset the sky stayed dark and several very black squalls made up in various parts of the horizon. The night, however, was not bad, and although the sky was very dark and the weather squally, we were obliged to shorten sail only to wait for the Naturaliste.

1801-01-18.journal_baudin: On the 28th [Nivôse, 18 January 1801] the weather continued to look bad until about three in the afternoon, when it cleared fine enough in the quarter of [blank], foretelling the winds from that point of the horizon, from which they did indeed come to us after sunset. During the day the ship was cleaned and fumigated throughout. We also set up our topmast shrouds and backstays, which needed it. At noon we had no observation of latitude. That by the reckoning of the run from the log was 52° 49' 31" South and the reckoned longitude 5° 18' 4" east. In the afternoon, although the weather had mended a little, we bent our storm sails in case we should need them during the night. A short time after sunset the sky turned dark again, very hazy and overcast. During the night the winds were variable from south to south-east, and I went on holding the east tack towards the north in the hope that the winds would come back to the south. During the night we had regulated our canvas so as to keep the Naturaliste at the same distance she was at the end of the day. Nevertheless at midnight, not seeing her, we clewed up our mainsail and made her various signals to get her to let us know her position, to which she did not answer, which obliged us to keep a light burning at the stern until daybreak. It appears that ship did not see our signals, for I must believe she would have answered had she known of them.

1801-01-19.journal_baudin: On the 29th [Nivôse, 19 January 1801] the weather was no finer than the day before. The sky in the forenoon was even more overcast and darker. The wind, however, was moderate and the heavy puffs that passed did not last long. At daylight we saw the Naturaliste very far to leeward of us; it seemed to us that ship, having been afraid of bad weather, had greatly shortened sail. To give her the means of closing us more quickly we bore down on her and at the same time took a second reef in the topsails. At noon the sun showed itself between the clouds and we observed its altitude which, though doubtful within a few minutes, was still better than our reckoning. The latitude was thus found to be 31° 46' 30", which gave us about one degree twelve minutes of northing in two days. Our longitude by the reckoning was then 7° 32' 24" east. As soon as the latitude was observed I made the signal to go about, and we took the south tack on the port tack. The winds came shortly afterwards from south-east to east-south-east. The sky was fine enough until three o'clock. At that hour the clouds had broken up in various parts of the horizon and we even reckoned on being able to observe a distance of the moon from the sun. Our hopes did not last long, for by four o'clock the weather was as dark and overcast as it had been for two days. The barometer, however, had risen a great deal, and the sea, though swelly, gave no sign of bad weather. At six o'clock I signalled the Naturaliste that if the winds came fair during the night we should steer south-east. The night of the 29th to the 30th [Nivôse, 19-20 January 1801] had nothing remarkable; we passed it under the foresail and close-reefed topsails to keep in sight of the Naturaliste, who was to leeward within gunshot. The sky was very overcast, we saw neither the moon nor the stars, and the gusts were less frequent than the night before.

1801-01-20.journal_baudin: On the 30th [Nivôse, 20 January 1801] the winds held steadily between east and south and were very variable. The sky seemed disposed to clear fine, and the clouds breaking up let us catch sight of the sun from time to time. The barometer, which had risen a great deal, also seemed to promise fine weather, and we hoped by that means to see the winds change. The sea too had gone down a great deal and we had almost lost that heavy south-west swell which had troubled us on the preceding days. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 10' 24" and the longitude by the reckoning 7° 3' 24" east. As no hour angle could be had that morning, we had no longitude from the watches. In the evening the sky, which had seemed inclined to clear, turned dark and overcast again, and we had now and then some gusts, but of little consequence and short duration. We went on holding the south tack, regulating ourselves by the Naturaliste's sailing, keeping her to leeward of us within gunshot. At six o'clock I signalled her that if the winds drew aft during the night we should steer south by east. This day we took a small marine animal which, without having the elegant shape or the brilliant colours of the lizard described by M. de la Martinière in Lapérouse's voyage, seemed to us far more interesting for its structure and the liveliness of its movements. The drawing I give of it is not perfect, because this animal changes shape so suddenly that it is impossible to seize one; but we recognised it plainly for a kind of mollusc which there is every reason to believe has not been observed up to this moment. I have put several specimens in spirits which seem likely to keep well, and perhaps on our return the naturalists will be able to make an exact description of them. We also took a kind of fucus which we did not know to what genus to refer. It was found to have various points of resemblance with the longissimus and the giganteus, but those two plants have not, in their description, all the particulars offered by the one of which I give the drawing. In the night of the 29th [Nivôse] to the 1st Pluviôse [20-21 January 1801] the sky stayed dark, overcast and damp. The cold was even rather sharp. The winds held, as during the day, between east and south and were very variable.

1801-01-21.journal_baudin: On the 1st Pluviôse [21 January 1801] the weather was the same as the day before; the sky, however, seemed at various times inclined to throw off the gloom that had hidden it from us for several days. In the forenoon we saw several albatrosses and some petrels of a species we had not yet noticed. There was some amusement on board in firing at several of them, but none was hit, although they were well within range. At noon we observed the latitude 34° 31' South, and the reckoned longitude was 6° 34' 24" east by the run measured with the log. That given by watch No. 31 was 3° 46' 56", and that deduced from No. 38, 3° 4' 56". In the afternoon, the weather having allowed us to take several distances of the moon from the sun, we found the longitude 3° 49' 30", which gave a difference from No. 31 of 2' 34" further west than that watch. During the evening the winds were as they had been in the morning, that is, very variable between east and south. The breeze we had during the day, though moderate, was not without unsteadiness, and we had several times some strong gusts, but of short duration. During the night the sky was dark and damp. The cold was even found rather sharp, although the thermometer had not fallen below thirteen degrees. The barometer, on the contrary, was beginning to rise and promised fine weather, as did the sea, whose swell and motion had much diminished. We went on holding the south tack under the courses and close-reefed topsails, this canvas being enough to keep way with the Naturaliste, who had all sail set.

1801-01-22.journal_baudin: On the 2nd [Pluviôse, 22 January 1801] in the morning the winds were less variable than on the preceding days and drew more to the east. The sky too was less overcast and we had the look of a fine day, but also of very little wind, and the sea foretold calm. About eight o'clock we spoke the Naturaliste and asked whether she could spare us a little rice, ours being so stowed that it has not been possible up to this moment to come at it. Captain Hamelin answered that he would send us some. His longitude, observed the day before by distances of the moon from the sun, was 2° 25' west of Paris, and that by his watches 2° 57', so that there was a considerable difference between the rate of his watches and his observations and ours, since it was, for the watches, 14' 44" taking a mean with ours, and by his observations 53' 45", taking likewise the mean of M. Gicquel's and my own. In the forenoon we had no hour angle to determine the rate of our watches since the last observation, but the latitude was found to be 35° 49' South. Our reckoning put us in 6° 38' 24" of east longitude. About three o'clock Captain Hamelin signalled to ask leave to send a boat on board, which was granted. By the letter he wrote me he let me know that all his crew and the naturalists were in good health and that good harmony and understanding reigned among them all. He added, however, that he had been obliged to have one of his seamen punished. He did not tell me for what cause. He also sent us a portion of the rice he had left. In the evening the weather was almost calm and the winds very variable. We took a great number of distances to check those of the day before, the mean result of which put us in 3° 5' 57". This day was very profitable for natural history: we took several new species of mollusc, a small fish of the greatest beauty, and a kind of shell that seemed to us entirely new. The animal it lodges is also very singular; it has the faculty of swimming, and even very fast, carrying its house with it. We took a great number of them. It appears this animal serves as food for various fish, for we recognised the same fragments of shell in the stomachs of those we had taken some days before. The coloured drawing I give of all these objects will make them far better known than any description I could make. Besides, I think the anatomists would have taken up that work, which properly belongs to them. Nevertheless I have preserved some in spirits for the Museum. After sunset the winds drew round to the north-east, and in the night they veered as far as west-south-west, where they stayed a short time before returning to the north. The breeze was light and the sky extremely damp, the horizon loaded with squalls that at times gave rain, but in small quantity. We shook out a reef from the topsails and went on steering south-east by east with the Naturaliste in our wake at a short distance.

1801-01-23.journal_baudin: On the 3rd [Pluviôse, 23 January 1801] in the forenoon the winds, which during the night had been from east round to north-west with a light breeze, drew successively from north-west to south-west. The sky, loaded with clouds that drove with great speed from that quarter, promised no fine weather, and the barometer had indeed fallen a great deal. About ten o'clock, the winds having drawn round to the south-west, it began to blow a fresh breeze, and it went on increasing until about four in the afternoon, when I had a second reef taken in the topsails to wait for the Naturaliste and to keep her from carrying too much sail to follow us, for at that hour she still had her topgallant sails set. At noon we observed the latitude 36° 13' South, and as no hour angle had been observed in the morning we had no longitude from the watches. That of the reckoning, without correction since our departure from Tenerife, was 7° 44' 44" east. In the afternoon it blew a strong breeze from south-south-west and the sea got up. At six o'clock I had the topgallant masts struck, and at seven a third reef was taken in the fore topsail. At that hour the Naturaliste was about half a league astern of us and in our wake. During the night of the 3rd to the 4th [Pluviôse, 23-24 January 1801] it continued to blow a strong breeze until about eleven o'clock, when the winds, having drawn round to the south, began to fall away. We kept our stern lantern lit all night, thinking the Naturaliste would do the same, or that at least she would show us a light from time to time to give us her position; but for all our care in watching for her we saw nothing. At midnight, although the wind had fallen a great deal, I had the mainsail furled, being persuaded that ship was astern. We lay thus waiting for her, the ship labouring a great deal for want of sail; and at four o'clock we were greatly astonished to see her half a league ahead of us and to windward. It appears she had concealed her sailing from us for the sorry pleasure of finding herself next morning ahead of us and to windward, while we had let ourselves be much knocked about by the sea in waiting for her.

1801-01-24.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 4th [Pluviôse, 24 January 1801] the winds were south, varying to south by west and at times south-south-west. The breeze was moderate and there was even the look of its falling further, but the sea was much agitated from the wind of the night and of the day before. We also had a heavy swell from the south-west that tried us a great deal. In the forenoon, however, we shook out a reef from the topsails and set the mizzen topsail, which had been furled the day before, as well as our staysails, in order to come up quickly with the Naturaliste, who was ahead of us. By noon we had closed her and passed her to leeward, to do her the honours of our sailing. At noon the observed latitude was 35° 49' South. Neither was there any longitude this day for the rate of the watches, no hour angle having been had. That of our reckoning put us in 10° 40' 36". In the afternoon until sunset the wind was slack and in the same quarter; the sea, still high and swelly, tried us a great deal and we felt at times some considerable rolling. During the night of the 4th to the 5th [Pluviôse, 24-25 January 1801] the winds were very variable from SSW to south-south-east; and as we carried little sail so as not to draw too far from the Naturaliste, the ship laboured a little in the heavy swell that was still running, though it had gone down a great deal from what it had been on the preceding days. During the day we had seen many albatrosses, petrels, and a kind of black gull with an entirely white belly whose flight came singularly close to that of the snipe. It was the first time we had seen this species of bird.

1801-01-25.journal_baudin: On the 5th [Pluviôse, 25 January 1801] the sky, though hazy and overcast, was less dark than it had been for several days, and we had hopes of being able to take an hour angle to get the longitude from our watches, of which we had been deprived for several days. In the forenoon the sky was fine enough and the winds south, variable to south-south-east. The weather was cold and everyone had got out his winter clothes. We were astonished to find the winds in this latitude so constant in the quarter from south towards east as they were; and as the moon's first quarter was past, we had no further hope of seeing them change before she came to the full. Well for us if our hopes are not disappointed. At noon, the sun being clear, we observed the latitude 35° 10' South, which gave us a difference of a few minutes from our reckoning. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 2° 11' 20" east, and for No. 38, 2° 55' 52" east. On board the Naturaliste they signalled us 2° 45', so that for a fortnight past their watches, which had always been nearly a degree ahead of ours, seemed to have lost considerably, which we put down to the change of temperature. By our reckoning from the log we were in 12° 30' 54" east, and consequently very near the Cape of Good Hope. In the evening the breeze fell away a great deal and there was even the look of calm for the night. At seven o'clock we bore down on the Naturaliste to close her, as she lay nearly a league to leeward. At eight, having got her into our wake, we resumed our course east-north-east, regulating our canvas by her sailing. In the night of the 5th to the 6th [Pluviôse, 25-26 January 1801] the winds were extremely variable, always from [blank] to SSE and yet at times south-south-west. We made little way, but on the other hand we were not a little tossed about by the sea, which had become swelly again. During the day several albatrosses and petrels had been seen, as well as gulls like those of the day before. Some claimed to have seen a pintado petrel, but I did not see it myself.

1801-01-26.journal_baudin: On the 6th [Pluviôse, 26 January 1801] in the forenoon the sky, though still half overcast, was fine enough. We could not, however, see the sun to observe an hour angle. The winds continued very variable, but at least they were from south to south-south-west; and though they were fair, the breeze was very light, and indeed we could not profit by it, being obliged to take in all our staysails to wait for the Naturaliste, who was far astern. During the forenoon we were obliged to break out part of our after hold to get at wine and other provisions we needed. At noon the observed latitude was 36° 45' South, which gave a single minute of difference from the reckoning. About ten o'clock we began to feel a very heavy swell from the south-west which, coming on us all at once, made us think that the wind sending it might not be far off and that we might soon see it arrive. The reckoned longitude at noon put us in 13° 54' 54". About three o'clock, the sun having shown itself, Citizen Bissy observed an hour angle which, referred to No. 38, the watch he uses, gave 4° 4' 54" of east longitude. In the evening we restowed our hold, and in doing that work we had the pleasure of coming upon one of our casks of rice which we had looked for in vain several times over. At sunset it continued to blow a light breeze from south-south-west, but in the night the winds veered to the south and it fell a good deal calmer. We steered close-hauled, taking care to keep a reasonable distance from the Naturaliste.

1801-01-27.journal_baudin: On the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1801] in the forenoon the winds were from south-east to south and nearly calm, and we made very little way. In the evening they drew round to the south-west and even west-south-west, but there was very little wind; we swayed up our topgallant masts to close the Naturaliste, who had gained a great deal on us by means of all her light sails. At eight o'clock we had her abeam, about half a league to leeward. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 36' 50" and the longitude by the reckoning 15° 9' 32" east, so that by our position from the log we were very near the Agulhas Bank; but as nothing gave us any sign of its nearness, we were not surprised to find ourselves still very far from it. By watch No. 31 the longitude was 4° 22' 15" east, and by No. 38, 5° 11' 2". The mean of these two watches, putting us in 4° 46' 38" 30‴, was much more likely than our reckoning, of which we had long made very little account. In the evening the weather turned fine, and the sky, which had long been covered with cloud and very dark to us, became clearer, and we had a fine sunset, which had not happened to us for many days. The air too had grown less cold. During the night of the 7th to the 8th [Pluviôse, 27-28 January 1801] the winds were variable from south-west to west-north-west, but there was so little wind that we did not go far. During the day of the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1801] we took various objects of natural history, the most interesting above all in the mollusc kind; the coloured drawings I give of them are made with the greatest exactness, and no doubt when they are seen it will be hard to believe that such things can exist. For what we took has far more likeness to a beautiful flower than to a living animal. After drawing these objects we put the marine animals into spirits; their shape has changed a great deal, but at least the gelatinous matter of which they are composed seems to have taken consistency enough to give hope of preserving them. It is particularly to Citizen Maugé that we shall owe the knowledge these captures may bring, for they were no doubt unknown until this moment.

1801-01-28.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 8th [Pluviôse, 28 January 1801], the Naturaliste being about three leagues ahead of us, I had the reefs shaken out of the main and fore topsails and we rigged out our studdingsail booms to starboard to join her. I still do not know for what reason she was allowed to draw so far off. In the forenoon the breeze was very light and we made little way. We were in no way compensated for the loss of this time by meeting with any new objects on the water, for we took only a single Portuguese man-of-war, though of a new species, whose filaments were ten or twelve feet long. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 21' 29" South, which gave us a considerable difference from our reckoning, since we found we had been set to the north 26' 9" more than we reckoned. The longitude given by No. 31, reduced to noon, was 4° 46' 43", and that of No. 38, 5° 31' 23", which gave a difference of rate between these watches of 0° 44' 40". In the afternoon, going through the log book kept by the officers, I noticed a remark I was far from expecting to find there. As Citizen Baudin had the watch from noon to four, I asked him, talking with him, by what singularity the Naturaliste had gained so much on us during the night. His answer was that we had carried little sail. I made him no other objection than this: who prevented you from making more? — and we changed the subject. I was far from having shown him any displeasure, the more so as the officer who had had the middle watch was perhaps as much in the wrong as he. Yet when I had gone back to my cabin he sent for the log book and entered a remark in it which I have struck out only in such a way that it can still be read. I asked him to explain his remark and what it was meant to say. His answer was that it was for the officer to whom he had handed over the watch, so that his answer, like his remark, was as meaningless as the other. In the afternoon the breeze continued very light.
